summary: This note is a Wikipedia-style overview of hearing loss, covering its definition, severity categories, types, and causes such as ageing, noise, genetics, infections and ototoxic drugs or chemicals. It also describes associated complications including cognitive decline, falls and depression, the difference between pre- and post-lingual deafness, and diagnosis, prevention, screening and management. The note states that about half of hearing loss is preventable and that hearing loss affected about 1.1 billion people as of 2013.
one_line: Overview of hearing loss: its definition, severity levels, types, causes, health complications, diagnosis, prevention, screening and management.
key_facts: Hearing loss is diagnosed when hearing testing finds a person is unable to hear 25 decibels in at least one ear.
Hearing loss is categorized as mild (25 to 40 dB), moderate (41 to 55 dB), moderate-severe (56 to 70 dB), severe (71 to 90 dB), or profound (greater than 90 dB).
As of 2013 hearing loss affects about 1.1 billion people to some degree, and causes disability in about 466 million people (5% of the global population).
Of those with moderate to severe disability, 108 million live in low and middle income countries.
Noise exposure is the cause of approximately half of all cases of hearing loss, causing some degree of problems in 5% of the population globally.
Around 75–80% of inherited hearing loss cases are inherited by recessive genes, 20–25% by dominant genes, 1–2% by X-linked patterns, and fewer than 1% by mitochondrial inheritance.
Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders are reported to cause hearing loss in up to 64% of infants born to alcoholic mothers.
The prevalence of hearing loss increases about two-fold for each decade increase in age after age 40.
About 9% of dementia cases are associated with hearing loss, according to the note.
Hearing loss is associated with Alzheimer's disease and dementia, and the risk increases with the degree of hearing loss.
The World Health Organization estimates that half of those between 12 and 35 are at risk from using personal audio devices that are too loud.
In the US, 12.5% of children aged 6–19 years have permanent hearing damage from excessive noise exposure.
Universal neonatal hearing screening rose in the US from less than 3% in the early 1990s to 98% in 2009.
Post-lingual deafness is far more common than pre-lingual deafness.
Non-signing (hearing) parents of deaf babies (90–95% of cases) usually go with the oral approach without sign language support.
Human hearing extends in frequency from 20 to 20,000 Hz, and hearing sensitivity peaks around 3,000 Hz.

entities.name: World Health Organization
entities.role: recommends limiting young people's exposure to loud sounds and personal audio players to an hour a day, and recommends immunization and premature birth prevention

entities.name: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health
entities.role: works with OSHA to provide standards and enforcement on US workplace noise levels; co-issued a 2018 bulletin on ototoxic chemicals

entities.name: Occupational Safety and Health Administration
entities.role: works with NIOSH on US workplace noise standards and enforcement; co-issued a 2018 informational bulletin on ototoxic chemicals

entities.name: United States Preventive Services Task Force
entities.role: recommends neonatal hearing screening for all newborns

entities.name: American Academy of Pediatrics
entities.role: advises that children have their hearing tested several times throughout their schooling

entities.name: American Language, Speech Pathology and Hearing Association
entities.role: recommends adults be screened at least every decade through age 50 and at three-year intervals thereafter

entities.name: Safe-in-Sound Award
entities.role: recognizes organizations that demonstrate successful noise control and other interventions in the workplace

entities.name: Buy Quiet program
entities.role: encourages employers to purchase quieter machinery and tools

entities.name: Healthy People 2020
entities.role: US Office of Disease Prevention and Health Promotion objectives including increasing the proportion of persons who have had a hearing examination

entities.name: World Hearing Day
entities.role: yearly event to promote actions to prevent hearing damage

entities.name: Alzheimer's disease
entities.role: condition associated with hearing loss in the note; association found nonsignificant for age-related hearing loss

entities.name: Deaf culture
entities.role: members may see themselves as having a difference rather than a disability and many oppose attempts to cure deafness
